body.statement:
Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\},
 \qquad
 \varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}=\frac{\nu}{8+4\nu}.
\]
Let \(0<\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\) and \(m_n\to\infty\) be deterministic.  The randomized-jitter Gaussian-multiplier set \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\) is implementable from the stratified observations and auxiliary standard normal draws.  Uniformly over the bounded ambient class \(\Theta\), including its no-breakout members,
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)
 \right|=0,
\]
where the probability is unconditional over the observations, all Gaussian multipliers, the observed-statistic jitter, and all Monte Carlo jitters.  The conclusion allows the same-sample estimated-\(A\) influence covariance \(\Sigma_n\) to be singular, to change rank with \(n\), or to equal zero, and it uses neither a covariance inverse nor a positive-eigenvalue bound.  Since \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\to0\), the randomization vanishes on the root-\(n\) projected-moment scale.  This is exact null calibration of an Anderson--Rubin inversion; no expected-length or diameter optimality is claimed for \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\).

There is a precise atomic limitation for deterministic single-threshold calibration.  If a reference statistic has distribution function \(F\), has an atom at a proposed cutoff \(x_0\), and
\[
 F(x_0-)<1-\alpha_0<F(x_0),
\]
then neither the deterministic rule accepting below \(x_0\) nor the deterministic rule accepting at or below \(x_0\) has acceptance probability \(1-\alpha_0\).  This limitation concerns only those deterministic single-threshold conventions at an atom; it is not an impossibility claim about every procedure without external randomization.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\mathcal K=\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), and use the block maximum norm in the randomized-inversion definition.  Its dimension
\[
 D_{\mathrm{AR}}=(E-1)(R_{\max}-d-1)
\]
is fixed.  All bounds below are uniform over \(\theta\in\Theta\).  By balanced shares, \(n_e\geq n\underline\pi\); hence every \(n_e\geq R_{\max}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).  The small-sample fallback is therefore well defined and eventually inactive.

At the true value \(b=\beta\), the ambient generated-projector expansion gives
\[
 H_n(\beta)=Z_n+R_n,
 \qquad
 Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}), \tag{1}
\]
where \(R_n=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly and
\[
 \Sigma_n=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}]. \tag{2}
\]
Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0,
 \qquad a=\nu/2.
\]
The construction in that lemma, the source moment envelope, the coefficient bounds, and \(\|C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\) give
\[
 \sup_{n,e,\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}\leq K. \tag{3}
\]
The division by \(\sigma_d(C)\) is licensed by the calibration-gap assumption.  No projected treatment contrast is divided by anywhere in this proof.

We first record rates for the observed Gaussian approximation.  Set
\[
 X_{e,i,n}=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}).
\]
Balanced shares and (3) imply
\[
 \sum_{e,i}\mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K n^{-\nu/2}. \tag{4}
\]
For a bounded one-Lipschitz function, Gaussian convolution at bandwidth \(s\), the second-order Taylor formula, and successive replacement by covariance-matched Gaussian summands give, exactly as in equations (24)--(27) of the ambient expansion proof,
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\{\mathcal L(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\}
 \leq K\{s+n^{-\nu/2}s^{-1-\nu}\}.
\]
Taking \(s=n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}\) yields
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\{\mathcal L_\theta(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\}
 \leq K n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}
 =K n^{-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}. \tag{5}
\]
This calculation uses only covariance matching and therefore permits singular \(\Sigma_n\).

We also need a rate for \(R_n\) because the jitter scale vanishes.  For every canonical projection of order \(j\geq2\), the equal-index-set calculation in the ambient expansion proof gives variance \(O(n_e^{-j})\) before root-\(n\) scaling and hence \(O(n^{-1})\) after that scaling.  The projector remainder on \(\{\|\widehat C-C\|\leq\kappa_0/2\}\) is bounded by \(K\sqrt n\|\widehat C-C\|^2\).  The first-projection representation and (3) imply
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat C-C\|^2\leq K/n,
 \qquad
 \Pr\{\|\widehat C-C\|>\kappa_0/2\}\leq K/n. \tag{6}
\]
On the exceptional event we truncate the distance at one.  Cauchy--Schwarz treats every product of two first-order estimation errors in the same way.  Summing the finitely many terms gives
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta[1\wedge\|R_n\|]
 \leq K n^{-1/2}. \tag{7}
\]
Consequently, adding \(R_n\) in (1) changes expectations of bounded one-Lipschitz functions by at most the left side of (7), and (5)--(7) give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\{\mathcal L_\theta(H_n(\beta)),N(0,\Sigma_n)\}
 \leq K n^{-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}. \tag{8}
\]
Here \(2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\leq1/2\), so the term in (7) is no larger in order than the displayed bound.

We next prove the quantitative estimated-influence replacement required for the conditional multiplier law.  For an order-\(s\) constituent kernel \(g\), define its population first projection by
\[
 \psi_{g,e}(w)=s\{\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb Eg\}.
\]
When \(s\geq2\), conditionally on \(W_{e,i}\), the leave-one-out average in \(\widehat\psi_{g,e,i}\) is an order-\((s-1)\) \(U\)-statistic based on the remaining observations.  In its conditional variance, disjoint tuples are conditionally independent, and there are \(O(n_e^{2s-3})\) overlapping pairs among \(O(n_e^{2s-2})\) ordered pairs.  The kernel second moment is bounded by (5) of the ambient expansion proof.  Thus the conditional-estimation error has unconditional second moment at most \(K/n_e\).  When \(s=1\), that conditional-estimation error is zero.  The same overlap count gives \(\mathbb E|U_{e,s}(g)-\mathbb Eg|^2\leq K/n_e\).  After applying the finitely many linear combinations and contrast signs, we obtain
\[
 \mathbb E R_n^\psi\leq K/n,
 \qquad
 R_n^\psi=\frac1n\sum_{e,i}\pi_e^{-2}
 \|\widehat\psi_{e,i}-\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2. \tag{9}
\]
Conditional Jensen's inequality applied to the leave-one-out averages and ordinary Jensen applied to the \(U\)-statistics also give uniform \((2+\nu)\)-moment bounds for both estimated and population first projections, because \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\).

Put \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\), \(\widehat h_k=\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k\), and
\[
 L_n^2=\|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 +\|\widehat C^\dagger-C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 +\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\|\widehat h_k-h_k\|^2. \tag{10}
\]
On \(\{\|\widehat C-C\|\leq\kappa_0/2\}\), the inverse identity and projector expansion give
\(\|\widehat C^\dagger-C^+\|+\|\widehat Q-Q_A\|\leq K\|\widehat C-C\|\).  Off this event, the threshold in the definition gives \(\|\widehat C^\dagger\|\leq2/\kappa_0\), while (6) controls the event.  The same \(U\)-statistic mean-square bounds control \(\widehat h_k-h_k\).  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E L_n^2\leq K/n,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E L_n\leq K n^{-1/2}. \tag{11}
\]
Define
\[
 Y_n=1+\frac1n\sum_{e,i}\pi_e^{-2}
 \{\|\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2+\|\widehat\psi_{e,i}\|^2\}.
\]
Since \(1+a=1+\nu/2\), Jensen's inequality for the empirical average and the \((2+\nu)\)-moment bounds give
\[
 \mathbb E Y_n^{1+a}\leq K. \tag{12}
\]
Adding and subtracting one factor at a time in the definitions of \(\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)\) and \(\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\), and using the uniform bounds on \(C^+\), \(\widehat C^\dagger\), and \(h_k\), yields the deterministic inequality
\[
 B_n:=\frac1n\sum_{e,i}\pi_e^{-2}
 \|\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)-\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2
 \leq K\{R_n^\psi+L_n^2Y_n\}. \tag{13}
\]
No independence between \(L_n\) and \(Y_n\) is used.

Define
\[
 \widetilde\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{e,i}\pi_e^{-2}
 \zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})^\top,
\]
and let \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)\) be the analogous empirical matrix formed from \(\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)\); this is exactly the conditional covariance of one multiplier draw.  The inequality
\(\|xx^\top-yy^\top\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|x-y\|(\|x\|+\|y\|)\), empirical Cauchy--Schwarz, and (13) give
\[
 \|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K\{(R_n^\psi Y_n)^{1/2}+L_nY_n+R_n^\psi+L_n^2Y_n\}. \tag{14}
\]
We integrate (14) explicitly.  For every \(t>0\), (9) and (12) imply
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge R_n^\psi Y_n]
 \leq t\mathbb ER_n^\psi+\Pr(Y_n>t)
 \leq K\{t/n+t^{-(1+a)}\}. \tag{15}
\]
Taking \(t=n^{1/(2+a)}\), followed by Jensen's inequality for the square root, gives
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge(R_n^\psi Y_n)^{1/2}]
 \leq K n^{-\kappa},
 \qquad
 \kappa=\frac{1+a}{2(2+a)}. \tag{16}
\]
Likewise, (11)--(12), without any independence assertion, give
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge L_nY_n]
 \leq t\mathbb EL_n+\Pr(Y_n>t)
 \leq K\{tn^{-1/2}+t^{-(1+a)}\}.
\]
With \(t=n^{1/\{2(2+a)\}}\), this is at most \(Kn^{-\kappa}\).  The same split with \(L_n^2\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge L_n^2Y_n]\leq K n^{-(1+a)/(2+a)},
\]
and (9) controls \(R_n^\psi\).  Therefore (14) implies
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]
 \leq K n^{-\kappa}. \tag{17}
\]

It remains to center the true-influence empirical covariance.  By (3), each matrix \(\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top\) has uniformly bounded \((1+a)\)-moment.  Truncate its norm at
\[
 \ell_n=n^{1/\{2(1+a)\}}.
\]
The mean norm of the discarded tail is at most \(K\ell_n^{-a}\).  In fixed dimension, the expected norm of the average of the centered truncated matrices is bounded by its root mean square, which is at most
\[
 K n^{-1/2}\ell_n^{(1-a)/2}
\]
after applying balanced shares.  This is no larger than the tail order.  Since \(\mathbb E\widetilde\Sigma_n=\Sigma_n\), we obtain
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 \|\widetilde\Sigma_n-\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K n^{-a/\{2(1+a)\}}
 =K n^{-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}. \tag{18}
\]
The identities
\[
 2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}=\frac{a}{2(1+a)},
 \qquad
 \kappa-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}
 =\frac{1}{2(2+a)(1+a)}>0 \tag{19}
\]
follow by direct algebra.  Because \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\) with \(\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\), equations (17)--(19) prove the required quantitative replacement:
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]=o(\tau_n^2), \tag{20}
\]
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]=o(\tau_n^2). \tag{21}
\]

Conditionally on the data, \(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\) is exactly Gaussian with covariance \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)\).  For positive semidefinite matrices \(S,T\), the integral representation
\[
 S^{1/2}=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}S(S+tI)^{-1}\,dt
\]
and the resolvent identity, split at \(t=\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), give
\[
 \|S^{1/2}-T^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}. \tag{22}
\]
The derivation does not require positive eigenvalues.  Couple the conditional multiplier Gaussian and \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\) as \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)^{1/2}Z\) and \(\Sigma_n^{1/2}Z\), with \(Z\sim N(0,I_{D_{\mathrm{AR}}})\).  Equations (21)--(22), truncation at distance one, and Jensen's inequality imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\{\mathcal L^*(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)),N(0,\Sigma_n)\}
 \leq K n^{-\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}=o(\tau_n). \tag{23}
\]

Now let \(G_n\sim N(0,\Sigma_n)\), let \(\xi\sim N(0,1)\) be independent, and define
\[
 F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)
 =\Pr\{\|G_n\|_{\max}+\tau_n\xi\leq t\}.
\]
For every \(t\), the function
\[
 x\longmapsto
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{t-\|x\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}\right)
\]
is bounded by one and has Lipschitz constant at most \((\sqrt{2\pi}\tau_n)^{-1}\).  Applying (8) and (23), and using \(\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\), yields
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta,t}
 \left|\Pr_\theta\{V_n(\beta)\leq t\}-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)\right|
 \longrightarrow0, \tag{24}
\]
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\sup_t
 \left|\Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\leq t\}-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)\right|
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{25}
\]
Indeed, the bounds are respectively \(O(n^{\chi-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}})\) and \(O(n^{\chi-\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}})\).

The ideal distribution function is continuous and strictly increasing even if \(\Sigma_n\) is singular or zero, because its density is
\[
 t\longmapsto
 \mathbb E\!\left[\tau_n^{-1}\phi\!\left(
 \frac{t-\|G_n\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}\right)\right]>0. \tag{26}
\]
Consequently, if \(V_n^\circ\) has distribution function \(F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}\), then \(1-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(V_n^\circ)\) is uniform on \((0,1)\).  The uniform distribution-function approximation (24) therefore implies
\[
 1-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(V_n(\beta))\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\).  Equation (25) shows, by evaluating the two conditional distribution functions at the random argument \(V_n(\beta)\), that the conditional upper-tail probability
\[
 p_n^*(\beta)=\Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\geq V_n(\beta)\}
\]
differs from \(1-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(V_n(\beta))\) by \(o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  The conditional comparison distribution is continuous because of its independent Gaussian jitter, so the weak inequality creates no tie term.  Hence
\[
 p_n^*(\beta)\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Unif}(0,1) \tag{27}
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\), including when \(\Sigma_n=0\) or changes rank.

Conditionally on the observations and \(\xi_0\), the \(m_n\) indicators defining \(\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)\) are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability \(p_n^*(\beta)\).  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
 \widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)\mid\text{observations},\xi_0
 \right)
 =\frac{p_n^*(\beta)\{1-p_n^*(\beta)\}}{m_n}
 \leq\frac1{4m_n}. \tag{28}
\]
Chebyshev's inequality and \(m_n\to\infty\) show that the Monte Carlo error is \(o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  Because \(\alpha_0\in(0,1/2)\) is a continuity point of the uniform distribution, (27)--(28) give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \left|\Pr_\theta\{\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)>\alpha_0\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{29}
\]
The event in (29) is exactly \(\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}\).  The probability integrates over the stratified observations, every multiplier, \(\xi_0\), and every Monte Carlo jitter.  This proves the asserted exact unconditional coverage.  Since \(\tau_n\to0\), both observed and multiplier jitters vanish on the root-\(n\) projected-moment scale.  Coverage alone supplies no expected-length or diameter assertion, so none is inferred.

Finally, suppose \(F\) has an atom at \(x_0\).  The deterministic strict single-threshold rule has acceptance probability \(F(x_0-)\), while the deterministic weak rule has acceptance probability \(F(x_0)\).  If
\[
 F(x_0-)<1-\alpha_0<F(x_0),
\]
neither probability equals \(1-\alpha_0\).  This proves exactly the stated limitation.  It does not exclude randomized acceptance on the equality event or other non-threshold procedures.
